```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6)

# --- Required packages ---
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(lubridate)
library(qgam)
library(plotly)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(sf)

# --- Figure export setup ---
dir.create("plots", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Centralised figure saving function.
# Change defaults here to modify all exported figures at once.
save_plot <- function(plot, filename, 
                      width = 10, height = 6, 
                      ext = c("pdf", "png"),
                      dpi = 300,
                      dir = "plots") {
  for (e in ext) {
    fpath <- file.path(dir, paste0(filename, ".", e))
    ggsave(fpath, plot = plot, width = width, height = height, dpi = dpi)
  }
  invisible(plot)
}

# Save interactive plotly widgets
save_widget <- function(widget, filename, dir = "plots") {
  fpath <- file.path(dir, paste0(filename, ".html"))
  htmlwidgets::saveWidget(widget, file = fpath, selfcontained = TRUE)
  invisible(widget)
}
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(base::as.factor)
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(base::intersect)
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)

```

## Preliminary analysis

In this preliminary analysis, we will seek to gain a rough understanding of the initial characteristics of the data we are using. We will begin by loading the important packages and the data.

The data has been loaded and preprocessed in a previous document. It consists of observations spanning from 2001 to 2022, at irregular intervals (2001, 2004, then biennially between 2004 and 2014, then annually from 2015 onwards). It is therefore sufficient to simply load the resulting file: 


```{r load_data}
Esca <- read.table(file = "data/Esca_CH_2001-2022.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",", 
                   dec = ".", na = "", stringsAsFactors = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(variety = gsub(x = variety, pattern = "_", replacement = " "),
         region = gsub(x = region, pattern = "_", replacement = " ")) |> 
  mutate(`Grouped variety` = if_else(variety %in% c("chasselas", "gamay", "pinot noir"), 
                                     true = variety, false = "Other variety")) |> 
  mutate(SymptApo = percentage_symptoms + percentage_apoplexy)

linewd <- 0.8
```

### Temporal evolution

One critical aspect is the temporal aspect. We are therefore initially interested in seeing whether we can visually observe a change in the proportion of vines affected.

```{r evolution_apoplexy, eval=FALSE}
year.br <- c(2001, 2004, seq(2006, 2022, by = 2))
year.lab <- as.character(year.br)

qfit <- qgam(percentage_apoplexy ~ s(Year), qu = .5,
             data = Esca |> select(Year, percentage_apoplexy) |> drop_na())
df.quant <- data.frame(Esca |> select(Year, percentage_apoplexy) |> drop_na(),
                       Quant = predict(qfit))

pl <- ggplot(Esca, aes(x = Year, y = percentage_apoplexy)) +
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(group = Year), outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = df.quant,
            aes(x = as.integer(as.factor(Year)), y = Quant, col = "smooth median"),
            linewidth = linewd) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = as.integer(as.factor(Year)), y = percentage_apoplexy,
                  col = "smooth mean"), se = FALSE, linewidth = linewd) +
  xlab("Year") + ylab("Apoplexy (%)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year.br, labels = year.lab) +
  scale_color_discrete("") +
  ggtitle("Proportion (%) of vine stock with apoplexy") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
print(pl)
save_plot(pl, "prop_evolution_apo")
save_widget(ggplotly(pl), "prop_evolution_apo")
```


We consider the sum of symptoms and apoplexy, which are the main indicators of Esca expression:

```{r evolution_symptapo}

df.quant <- data.frame(Year = with(Esca, seq(min(Year), max(Year), by = 0.25)))
df.quant <- cbind.data.frame(df.quant, Quant = predict(object = qfit, newdata = df.quant))

pl <- ggplot(Esca, aes(x = Year, y = SymptApo)) + 
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(group = Year), outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = df.quant, 
            aes(x = Year, y = Quant, col = "smooth median"),
            linewidth = linewd) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = Year, y = SymptApo, col = "smooth mean"), 
              se = FALSE, linewidth = linewd) +
  xlab("Year") + ylab("Symptoms + Apoplexy (%)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year.br, labels = year.lab) +

  ggtitle("Proportion (%) of vine stock with symptoms or apoplexy") +

print(pl)
save_plot(pl, "prop_evolution_SympApo")
save_widget(ggplotly(pl), "prop_evolution_SympApo")
```

### Regional differences

```{r evo_region_sympt, fig.height=7, eval=FALSE}
dat_reg <- Esca |> 
  select(Year, percentage_symptoms, region) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(region = factor(region))

qfit <- qgam(percentage_symptoms ~ s(Year, region, bs = "fs"), qu = .5, data = dat_reg, control = list(progress = "none"))
df.quant <- dat_reg |> mutate(Quant = predict(qfit))

pl <- ggplot(dat_reg, aes(x = as.factor(Year), y = percentage_symptoms)) + 
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  geom_line(data = df.quant, 
            aes(x = as.integer(as.factor(Year)), y = Quant, col = "smooth median"),
            linewidth = linewd) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = as.integer(as.factor(Year)), y = percentage_symptoms, col = "smooth mean"), 
              se = FALSE, linewidth = linewd) +
  xlab("Year") + ylab("Symptoms (%)") +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = year.br, labels = year.lab) + 
  scale_color_discrete("") +
  ggtitle("Proportion (%) of vine stock with symptoms — by region") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 8)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
print(pl)
save_plot(pl, "prop_evolution_sympt_regions", height = 7)
save_widget(ggplotly(pl), "prop_evolution_sympt_regions")
```

In terms of grape varieties, sauvignon blanc appears more sensitive than other varieties. However, the small number of samples does not allow a decisive conclusion (< ~1% of the sample). Furthermore, this variety is only found in certain regions, so it is difficult to separate variety sensitivity from regional effects. In the following analysis and because of the very low number of observations, we will **exclude the plots with sauvignon blanc**. The plot also has a particular history that may explain a particular behavior.


### Maps

```{r maps, fig.height=10, results='asis'}
maps_available <- tryCatch({
  source("map_Esca_sampling_plots.R")
  TRUE
}, error = function(e) {
  cat("\n\n*Maps not rendered: external map data unavailable.*\n\n")
  FALSE
})

if (maps_available) {
  # Ensure coordinates are in LV95
  if (all(floor(log10(abs(c(Esca$E[!is.na(Esca$E)], Esca$N[!is.na(Esca$N)])))) == 5, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    Esca <- Esca |> mutate(E_lv95 = E + 2e6, N_lv95 = N + 1e6)
  } else {
    Esca <- Esca |> mutate(E_lv95 = E, N_lv95 = N)
  }
  
  # year_plot <- sort(unique(Esca$Year))
  # year_plot <- year_plot[seq(3, length(year_plot), by = 3)]
  year_plot <- c(2001, 2012, 2022)
  for (yr in year_plot) {
    Esca_plt <- Esca |> 
      filter(Year == yr) |> 
      select(plot, region, commune, Year, percentage_apoplexy, percentage_symptoms, SymptApo, E_lv95, N_lv95) |> 
      rename(x = E_lv95, y = N_lv95)
    pl_SymptApo <- maps_year_Zoom_Altitude(
        data = Esca_plt |> rename(z = SymptApo),
        lab_scale = "Symptoms + apoplexy (%)")
    # pl_apo <- maps_year_Zoom_Altitude(
    #   data = Esca_plt |> rename(z = percentage_apoplexy), 
    #   lab_scale = "apoplexy (%)")
    # pl_sympt <- maps_year_Zoom_Altitude(
    #   data = Esca_plt |> rename(z = percentage_symptoms), 
    #   lab_scale = "symptoms (%)")
    
    # combined <- pl_apo / pl_sympt + 
    combined <- pl_SymptApo +
          plot_annotation(title = paste0("Apoplexy and symptoms, ", yr))
    print(combined)
    save_plot(combined, paste0("map_", yr), width = 10, height = 10)
  }
  
  # Median maps for stable plots
  df_median2012 <- Esca |> 
    filter(stable_group == "2012-2022" & Year >= 2012) |> 
    group_by(plot, region, E_lv95, N_lv95) |> 
    summarise(MedianSymptApo = median(SymptApo), .groups = "drop") |> 
    rename(x = E_lv95, y = N_lv95, z = MedianSymptApo)
  
  pl_med <- maps_year_Zoom(data = df_median2012, 
                           lab_scale = "Median (%) 2012-2022", xupperbnd = 3) + 
    ggtitle("Median Symptoms + Apoplexy", subtitle = "Stable plots: 2012-2022")
  print(pl_med)
  save_plot(pl_med, "map_median_2012_2022")
}
```


## Stable plots

Among the whole data set, some plots have been in the data set for a long period. We consider the subset for which we have complete data from 2004 to 2022.

```{r stable_plots, fig.height=7}

  filter(stable_group == "2004-2022", Year >= 2004) |>  
  mutate(region = factor(region))


qfit <- qgam(SymptApo ~ s(Year, region, bs = "fs"), qu = .5, data = dat_stable, control = list(progress = "none"))
df.quant <- dat_stable |> mutate(Quant = predict(qfit))

pl1 <- ggplot(dat_stable |> select(Year, SymptApo, region) |> drop_na(),

  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(group = Year), outlier.alpha = 0.3) +

            linewidth = linewd) +

              se = FALSE, linewidth = linewd) +
```

## Correlation Analysis

We compute the Spearman rank correlation between the response variable (Symptoms + Apoplexy %) and all climatic predictors. This measure captures monotonic associations.

```{r corr_load_data, include=FALSE}
source("esca_ml_config.R")
source("esca_ml_pipeline.R")

# Load full dataset with merged weather
corr_data <- load_esca_data(config = config_full_dataset())
```

### Monthly variables

```{r corr_monthly, fig.height=8, fig.width=10}
library(corrplot)

# Select monthly climate columns and the response
month_labels <- month(3:10, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
monthly_vars <- c(
  paste0("Temperature_", month_labels),
  paste0("Humidity_", month_labels),
  paste0("Precipitation_", month_labels),
  paste0("Evapotranspiration_", month_labels),
  paste0("Radiation_", month_labels),
  paste0("Pressure_", month_labels),
  paste0("VPD_", month_labels)
)

# Add contrast variable
monthly_vars <- c(monthly_vars, "Contrast_MayJune_VPD")

# Keep only columns that exist in the data
monthly_vars <- intersect(monthly_vars, names(corr_data))
monthly_cols <- c("SumSymptApo", monthly_vars)

corr_monthly_df <- corr_data |>
  select(all_of(monthly_cols)) |>
  drop_na()

corr_monthly_mat <- cor(corr_monthly_df, method = "spearman")

# Extract only the correlations with the response variable
corr_with_response <- corr_monthly_mat["SumSymptApo", -1, drop = FALSE]
corr_sub <- corr_monthly_mat[c("SumSymptApo", monthly_vars), c("SumSymptApo", monthly_vars)]

corrplot(corr_sub, method = "color", type = "lower",
         tl.cex = 0.6, tl.col = "black", cl.cex = 0.7,
         title = "Spearman Correlation — Monthly Climate Variables",
         mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
```

#### Interpretation

With **monthly** climate variables (~56 predictors), FORD identifies **VPD in July** and **Humidity in June** as the only two variables with a statistically significant signal beyond random noise.

With **seasonal** aggregates (~7 predictors), FORD selects **SeasVPD** (seasonal mean of maximum daily VPD) as the sole significant variable. This is consistent: VPD in July is the dominant monthly contributor to the seasonal VPD aggregate.

In both cases, VPD-related variables emerge as the strongest model-free signal, confirming the model-based importance rankings (see below) where VPD and humidity-related variables consistently appear among the top predictors.

#### Testing the "cold-wet → hot-dry" transition hypothesis

It has been suggested in the literature that Esca expression is linked to abrupt transitions from cold-wet to hot-dry conditions, particularly between May and June (Bortolami et al., *PNAS*, 2021). To challenge this hypothesis, we introduced a contrast variable:

- **`Contrast_MayJune_VPD`** = VPD~June~ − VPD~May~ — captures the abrupt shift in atmospheric water demand between May and June. A large positive value indicates a rapid transition from cool/humid to hot/dry conditions.

This variable is included in both the monthly and seasonal FORD analyses. If the hypothesis holds, FORD should detect this contrast as a significant predictor of Esca expression. The Spearman correlations in the preceding section provide an initial assessment of the strength and direction of this association.

### Algorithm description

**FORD** (Feature Ordering by Integrated $R^2$ Dependence is a model-agnostic variable selection algorithm that identifies statistically significant predictors without relying on any specific model or assumptions. See the reference for more details.  

The method works by comparing each variable's conditional dependence with the response. Variables are selected sequentially: at each step, the variable most associated with the response is chosen, and the procedure stops when no remaining variable are positively associated in the sense of the integrated $R^2$ measure.

**Reference**: Azkadia, M. and Roudaki, P. (2025). *A new measure of dependence: Integrated $R^2$*, .




## Predictive Modelling

### Pipeline overview

A machine learning pipeline was developed to predict Esca disease expression (`SumSymptApo` = sum of symptoms and apoplexy percentages) from climatic and soil variables. The pipeline uses the `tidymodels` framework and proceeds as follows:

1. **Data splitting**: 75% training / 25% test set (stratified by response)
2. **Preprocessing**: Missing value filtering, near-zero variance removal, centering/scaling, dummy encoding of categorical variables
3. **Models trained**:
   - **Random Forest** (ranger) -- 27 hyperparameter combinations
   - **Gradient Boosting** (XGBoost) -- 64 hyperparameter combinations  
   - **LASSO regression** (glmnet) -- 20 penalty values
4. **Tuning**: 10-fold cross-validation on the training set
5. **Evaluation**: Final models refit on full training data and evaluated on held-out test set

### Data sources

Climate data comes from two networks:

- **MeteoSwiss** (Federal Office of Meteorology): ~8 stations in the study area, complete temporal coverage 2001-2024. Measured variables: temperature, pressure, precipitation, radiation, humidity, evapotranspiration.
- **Vitimeteo** (Agrometeo network, Agroscope): ~41 stations, closer to vineyard plots but with data gaps (no data before 2003, some station interruptions). Same variable types excluding pressure.

The pipeline uses a **Vitimeteo-first with MeteoSwiss fallback** merging strategy: for each plot-year combination, Vitimeteo data is used if the nearest station is within 30 km and data is available; otherwise, MeteoSwiss data from the closest station is used.

**VPD** (Vapour Pressure Deficit) is computed from hourly temperature and humidity data using the Tetens formula, then aggregated as the maximum daily VPD averaged over each month.

All climate variables are aggregated **monthly** over the growing season (March-October), yielding 8 values per variable type. Additionally, **seasonal aggregates** (`SeasXX`) summarise the entire growing season into a single value per variable.

**Soil data**: Available water reserve (`RU_nb`) from soil surveys.

### Baseline

The baseline predictor uses the **overall mean** of the training set as the prediction for all test observations. This represents the simplest possible prediction -- without any climatic or soil information -- and serves as the reference against which ML models are evaluated.

### Results

```{r ml_results}
perf_file <- "results/combined_performance_summary.csv"
if (!file.exists(perf_file)) {
  cat("*ML results not available. Run `source('run_all_configurations.R')` first.*\n")
  knitr::knit_exit()
}

perf_all <- read_csv(perf_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Order configurations so that monthly appears in the left column and seasonal
# in the right column when using facet_wrap(ncol = 2)
# Interleave: monthly1, seasonal1, monthly2, seasonal2, ...
monthly_configs <- sort(unique(perf_all$configuration[!grepl("Seasonal", perf_all$configuration)]))
seasonal_configs <- sort(unique(perf_all$configuration[grepl("Seasonal", perf_all$configuration)]))
config_order <- as.vector(rbind(monthly_configs, seasonal_configs))

perf_all <- perf_all |>
  mutate(configuration = factor(configuration, levels = config_order))

baseline <- perf_all |> filter(model == "baseline_year_region")
models <- perf_all |> filter(model != "baseline_year_region")

baseline_wide <- baseline |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = value) |>
  select(config_id, configuration, baseline_rmse = rmse, baseline_mae = mae)

models_wide <- models |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = value) |>
  left_join(baseline_wide |> select(-configuration), by = "config_id") |>
  mutate(
    configuration = factor(configuration, levels = config_order),
    mae_vs_baseline = (mae - baseline_mae) / baseline_mae * 100,
    rmse_vs_baseline = (rmse - baseline_rmse) / baseline_rmse * 100
  )
```

#### Performance summary (MAE focus)

The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) represents the average absolute difference between predicted and observed disease expression, in percentage points. A model with MAE = 1.5 means predictions are on average 1.5 percentage points away from the truth.

```{r ml_table}
summary_table <- models_wide |>
  arrange(configuration, mae) |>
  mutate(
    mae_delta = paste0(ifelse(mae_vs_baseline > 0, "+", ""), round(mae_vs_baseline, 1), "%")
  ) |>
  select(Configuration = configuration, Model = model,
         MAE = mae, `Delta MAE vs baseline` = mae_delta,
         RMSE = rmse, `R2` = rsq) |>
  left_join(
    baseline_wide |> select(Configuration = configuration, `Baseline MAE` = baseline_mae),
    by = "Configuration"
  )

kable(summary_table, digits = 3,
      caption = "Test-set performance. Delta MAE shows % change relative to baseline (negative = better).")
```

### Key findings

```{r key_findings}
best <- models_wide |> slice_min(mae, n = 1)
```

- **Best overall model**: `r best$model` on *`r best$configuration`* -- MAE = `r round(best$mae, 2)` (percentage points), representing a `r round(abs(best$mae_vs_baseline), 1)`% improvement over the baseline.
- **Seasonal precipitation** (`SeasPrecipitation`) and **VPD** (`SeasVPD`) are consistently the most important climatic predictors across all configurations and models.
- Using **seasonal aggregate** features (instead of monthly values) improves performance for the "Stable Chasselas" configuration, suggesting that for well-characterised plots, the overall seasonal climate signal is more predictive than month-by-month detail.
- Random Forest and Gradient Boosting consistently outperform the baseline and LASSO, indicating non-linear relationships between climate and disease expression.


### Combined variable importance

Individual model importance scores use different scales (permutation importance for RF, gain for XGBoost, absolute coefficients for LASSO). To obtain a unified ranking, we apply the following procedure. Let us denote the set of models by $M$ and the set of variables (that can depend of the model considered) by $I$. 

1. **Rescale** each model's importance to [0, 1] by dividing by the maximum within that model. We thus get a set of scores $s_i^m\in [0,1]$ for each $i\in I$ and $m\in M$. 
2. **Weight** each model proportionally to its MAE improvement over the baseline:
$$w_m = \max\!\big(0,\; (\text{MAE}_{\text{baseline}} - \text{MAE}_m) / \text{MAE}_{\text{baseline}}\big).$$
Models that do not beat the baseline receive zero weight.
3. **Combine** via weighted average:
$$
\text{Combined}_i = \dfrac{\sum_m w_m \, s_i^m}{\sum_m w_m}.
$$


```{r combined_vimp_comparison, fig.height=5}
# Side-by-side: top 10 from each aggregation mode

  filter(aggregation == "Monthly") |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(importance = mean(combined_importance), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(importance, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>

  filter(aggregation == "Seasonal") |>
  group_by(Variable) |>

  mutate(Variable = fct_reorder(Variable, importance)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Variable, y = importance, fill = mode)) +

       x = NULL, y = "Combined importance (0-1 scale)") +

```

In both aggregation modes, **VPD** (Vapour Pressure Deficit) emerges as the most influential climate variable. In the monthly setting, VPD in April, July and October are the top predictors, along with atmospheric pressure during the growing season. In the seasonal setting, `SeasVPD` consistently dominates, followed by `SeasPrecipitation` and `SeasPressure`. The soil water reserve (`RU_nb`) also appears in several seasonal configurations, confirming that water availability -- both atmospheric (VPD) and edaphic (soil reserve) -- is the primary driver of Esca expression.

```{r plot VPD grid}
RelHum_grid <- seq(50, 100, by = 10)

df_grid <- expand.grid(Temperature = temp_grid, RelHum=RelHum_grid)
df_grid <- df_grid |>   mutate(VPD = 0.611 * exp((17.27 * Temperature)/ (237.3 + Temperature))) |> 
  mutate(VPD = VPD * (1- RelHum/100)) 

ggplot(data = df_grid, aes(x = Temperature, y = VPD, col = as.factor(RelHum))) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_discrete("Relative Humidity") +
  ggtitle(label = "VPD", subtitle = "In terms of temperature and relative humidity")

```

```{r vpd_scatter, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=9}

# SeasVPD is computed from monthly VPD columns during load_merged_weather_data()
pl_vpd <- full_data |>
  filter(!is.na(SeasVPD), !is.na(SumSymptApo)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = SeasVPD, y = SumSymptApo)) +

       subtitle = "Each point = one plot-year observation",

  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"))

pl_vpd
```

---


## Conclusions and take home message

From the data, we can conclude that

- There is **no evidence of a negative evolution of the incidence of the esca disease over the years**, not globally, nor by region.
- There are strong regional differences, that only partially explained by the meteorological conditions. Some other factors, such as the pedology, the variety, the rootstock are certainly playing an important role that cannot be highlighted with the data at hand.

Regarding the climatic variable having an influence on the expression of the esca disease:

1. Results must be interpreted **with care**. The predictive power is low, and the results must be considered with care and only in comparison with other papers.  Esca expression has high inherent variability, even given meteorological data.
2. VPD is the primary environmental driver of Esca expression. However, this being a function of both relative humidity and temperature.
3. Water stress (VPD + precipitation + soil reserve) seems to be the "fil rouge"  across all analyses focusing on variable importance.
4. In the monthly dataset, we observe some spurious correlations. Since the observations were all made in late August, the fact that monthly variables of September and October appear can only be an artifact. This cast doubts about the results. 

## Relation to the literature

The results are essentially in line with the literature. 


- High VPD -> less esca. In line with [Bortolami et al. (PNAS, 2021)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2112825118)
- Correlations similar to those described in [F. Calzarano et al. (Phytopathologia Mediterranea, 2018)]
(https://doi.org/10.14601/Phytopathol_Mediterr-23787)
- Relation to Water Holding Soil Capacity not clear but **data are scarce**. Other aspects in line with [Monod et al. , 2023](https://doi.org/10.20870/oeno-one.2025.59.1.7659), while some others are not corroborated. 


>Esca incidence was correlated with precipitation, 
particularly in May and June by our regression analyses 
(Figure 9). Previous studies have mentioned that cool, 
rainy summers favour the expression of esca leaf symptoms 
(Surico et al., 2000; Marchi et al., 2006) and especially the 
rainfall pattern from May to July (Calzarano et al., 2018b), 
which is consistent with our results. According to our 
observations, the years characterised by the highest rainfall 
are those in which the incidence of esca is the highest across 
the network of vineyards (years 2019 and 2021; Figures 4 
and 5). Hot and dry summers are considered to favour 
apoplexy (Surico et al., 2000; Marchi et al., 2006). The 
appearance of apoplectic events was not linked with hot and 
dry weather in our observations. On the contrary, the year 
2018 was particularly hot and dry during the summer and 
was the year with the lowest number of apoplectic events and foliar symptom rates (Figures 3 and 4). The year 2021 was 
the wettest year with the highest number of foliar symptoms 
and apoplectic events in three of the four viticultural regions 
monitored. Both years 2019 and 2021 were characterised by 
a particularly rainy and cold May, followed by a hot (2019) 
or rainy and hot (2021) summer. These observations align 
with earlier research, including Surico et al. (2000), which 
proposed a relation between apoplexy and alternating periods 
of dry, hot weather and wet, cool conditions. Such weather 
patterns promote vigorous leaf and canopy growth, leading 
to high evapotranspiration rates, and potentially disrupting 
sap flow (McDowell et al., 2008)
